title: The Krobo: The People of the Mountain

pages.text: On the road from Tema to Akosombo, just before Akuse junction, a single mountain rises steeply from the flat Accra plains. Its sides are almost cliffs. Baboons live among its rocks. On most days nobody is there. But each year, in October and November, thousands of people in fine cloth and strings of glass beads climb its paths. They visit the stone remains of houses, pour libation, and tell their children: this is where we come from. They are the Krobo, and for about five hundred years this mountain was their home.

pages.alt: A steep, lone mountain rising from flat grassland, with a line of people climbing a path up its side.

pages.text: The Krobo are a Dangme people, related to the Ga. Tradition says that their ancestors came from the east and, looking for a safe place, chose the mountain. They called it Klowem. On its top they built towns of stone houses with narrow lanes between them. The steep slopes made a natural fortress, and the few paths were easy to defend. Asante and Akwamu armies tried to take the mountain and failed. The people were led at first by priests. Later, chiefs called konors ruled two divisions: Manya Krobo and Yilo Krobo.

pages.text: A mountain top has little farmland, so the Krobo farmed the plains below and returned home to the mountain. As their numbers grew, they needed more land. They did not go to war for it. Groups of families put their money together and bought long strips of forest land from their Akan neighbours. They cleared it, planted it, and then bought the next strip. This system was called huza. In this way the Krobo spread north and west and became great producers of palm oil, which factories in Europe wanted for soap and for oiling machines.

pages.text: By the 1850s, the British controlled the coast and wished to tax the people. The Krobo refused to pay, and soldiers were sent. The British then fined the Krobo a huge sum, and told them to pay it in palm oil, sold to chosen merchants at a low price. The Krobo answered in a way their rulers did not expect. They stopped selling palm oil altogether. For several years they sent their oil by other routes or kept it at home. The merchants lost money, and in the end the government had to give up the scheme.

pages.text: The mountain towns worried the colonial government. It could not easily watch what went on there, and missionaries disliked the old religious rites. In 1892, the governor gave an order: everyone must leave the mountain within three days. Soldiers then destroyed the houses. It was a bitter day. The Krobo carried what they could down to their farm villages on the plain. These grew into the towns of Odumase and Somanya. They had lost their home, but they had not lost their land, their language, or their skills, and they prospered.

pages.text: Today the Krobo are famous for glass beads. Bead makers crush old bottles, fill clay moulds with the powder, and fire them in ovens to make beads of every colour. The beads are worn at festivals and at the ceremonies that mark a girl’s passage into womanhood. And every year the people climb Klowem again: Manya Krobo for the Ngmayem festival and Yilo Krobo for Kloyosikplem. Their history shows three ways to be strong without an army: choose your ground wisely, pool your money and buy, and when treated unfairly, refuse together.

activities.question: Why did the Krobo choose to live on the mountain?
options: The soil on top was the best for farming
Its steep sides made it easy to defend
It was close to the sea

activities.question: How did the Krobo gain more farmland?
options: Groups of families pooled their money and bought land strip by strip
The British gave it to them

activities.question: How did the Krobo respond to the unfair fine?
options: They refused to sell palm oil until the scheme was dropped

activities.question: Apply it: Ten farmers each have too little money to buy a tractor. Which Krobo idea could help them?
options: Each should wait until he is rich
Pool their money, buy one together, and share its use
